newsitem.title: SPAIN: NATO set for discordant summit on enlargement.
newsitem.headline: NATO set for discordant summit on enlargement.

text.p: In Cold War days, NATO summits were choreographed rituals at which grateful European allies rallied behind the United States in displays of unity and resolve.

But the 16-nation summit which opens in Madrid on Tuesday with a bold agenda of extending the Western alliance into former communist central and eastern Europe and reforming NATO's structures could be unusually discordant.

The United States, with the self-assurance of the world's sole remaining superpower, has sought to impose its view of the new European security order single-handedly, decreeing that only three former Warsaw Pact states -- Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary -- may join NATO in the first wave.

Nine European allies, led by France and Italy, want Romania and Slovenia be added to that list, arguing that they qualify both as democratic market economies and as states in need of security on the edge of Black Sea and Balkan danger zones.

President Bill Clinton, who spent the weekend relaxing with King Juan Carlos on the Spanish holiday island of Majorca, made clear before leaving Washington he would not allow more than three entrants now.

Only those three, which happen to have influential ethnic lobbies in the United States, were ready politically and militarily, he argued. The Republican-dominated U.S. Congress is concerned about the cost of a wider enlargement.

NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana said on Saturday there was no consensus yet on the number of states to be admitted, nor on any assurance to be given to those who do not join in the first wave, probably in 1999.

Nevertheless, U.S. officials said they did not expect public hostility from the European allies, except for France, which has another quarrel with Washington over its spurned demand for NATO's southern command, which controls the Mediterranean, to be handed over to a European. Clinton has refused.

"We expect the French to be the French," a U.S. official said, resigned to a likely blast from President Jacques Chirac, who has said France's conditions for rejoining NATO's military wing have not been met.
However, Chirac's spokesman said on Friday that Paris would not "take hostage" the three countries to which all agree just to press for the inclusion of Romania and Slovenia.
Even if only the three favourites get the nod, Solana said he was convinced the outcome would enhance security deep into eastern Europe by extending NATO's zone of stability.
"Out of this alliance and out of this summit, everybody will be a winner from the point of view of security. No country will be a loser," he told a Madrid news conference on Saturday.
"We are not going to create new divisions in Europe. On the contrary, we are going to erase them."

Russian President Boris Yeltsin signed the Founding Act of a new, cooperative relationship with NATO at a summit in Paris in May, assuaging Moscow's continued hostility to the Western alliance's expansion into its former satellites.

To avoid being seen to give his blessing to enlargement, Yeltsin decided not to come to Madrid, where 28 east European nations will join the 16 NATO leaders for the first meeting of a new Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council on Wednesday.

An overhaul of NATO's military commands to streamline the organisation for post-Cold War rapid deployment, peacekeeping and humanitarian missions will not be completed in Madrid, largely because of the dispute with France.

Instead, officials said some principles would be approved, such as the appointment of a European deputy supreme commander empowered to run European missions using NATO assets if the United States chooses not to get involved. He will be able to call on a European chain of command within the NATO structure.

While France is staying out of the military structure which it quit in 1966, summit host Spain, which joined NATO in 1982 after its transition to democracy, is expected to announce its readiness to go forward with full integration with the command.

Although only about 1,000 leftists turned out for an anti-NATO demonstration on Saturday, Spanish security forces are taking no chances, with more than 4,000 police on duty and armoured cars posted at key targets such as the U.S. embassy.
Police also put into place anti-terrorist contingency plans and were on alert for any action by the Basque separatist guerrilla group ETA.
